bib.title: High-Probability Lower Bounds (Chapter 17, Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press (book chapter)

question: Can a single bandit policy with a good expected-regret bound also have a high-probability regret bound that is better than the lower bounds, in stochastic and adversarial settings?
contributions: Theorem 17.1 and Corollaries 17.2, 17.3: high-probability lower bound for stochastic Gaussian bandits given a worst-case expected-regret guarantee
Theorem 17.4: high-probability lower bound sqrt(nk log(1/(2 delta))) for adversarial bandits
Notes: the Exp3-IX high-probability upper bounds of Chapter 12 are tight up to constants

results.claim: A policy whose expected regret is at most B*sqrt((k-1)n) on every k-armed Gaussian bandit with gaps at most one has some bandit where the random pseudo-regret exceeds (1/4)min{n,(1/B)sqrt((k-1)n log(1/(4 delta)))} with probability at least delta (Theorem 17.1).
results.setup: Class E_k of k-armed Gaussian bandits with suboptimality gaps bounded by one; n>=1, k>=2, B>0, delta in (0,1); policy with R_n<=B sqrt((k-1)n) for all nu in E_k.
results.note: Proved in text; proof uses Lemma 4.5, Bretagnolle-Huber (Thm 14.2), divergence decomposition (Lemma 15.1), a bandit with mu_1=Delta and a perturbed arm mu_i+2Delta.

results.claim: No policy can satisfy P(pseudo-regret >= B sqrt((k-1)n) log^p(1/delta)) < delta for all n, delta, and all nu in E_k with p in (0,1): the sqrt(log(1/delta)) tail behaviour of the delta-free Exp3-IX bound cannot be improved to a log^p tail with p<1 (Corollary 17.3).
results.setup: Same class E_k, k>=2, B>0, p in (0,1); proof by contradiction, integrating the tail to bound expected regret by B sqrt(n(k-1)) then applying Theorem 17.1.

results.claim: Corollary 17.2: if n*delta <= sqrt(n(k-1)log(1/(4delta))), every policy has a bandit in E_k with P(pseudo-regret >= (1/4)min{n, sqrt(n(k-1)/2 log(1/(4delta)))}) >= delta.
results.setup: Any policy, any n>=1,k>=2, delta satisfying (17.6); proof sets B=sqrt(2 log(1/(4delta))) since expected regret <= n delta + sqrt(n(k-1)/2 log(1/(4delta))).

results.claim: For adversarial bandits, for n >= C k log(1/(2 delta)) there is a reward sequence x in [0,1]^{n x k} where regret exceeds c sqrt(nk log(1/(2 delta))) with probability at least delta, for any algorithm (Theorem 17.4).
results.setup: Any policy; c,C universal constants; rewards in [0,1]; proof only sketched (via truncated-normal random reward sequence Q_i, Claims 17.5-17.7, refers to Gerchinovitz and Lattimore 2016).
results.note: Claim 17.6 uses Delta = sigma sqrt((k-1)/(2n) log(1/(8 delta))); Claim 17.7 needs sigma=1/10, Delta<1/8, n>=32 log(1/delta).

results.claim: Knowing the confidence level in advance really does help: the Exp3-IX bound O(sqrt(kn log(k/delta))) for a delta-specific algorithm and the anytime bound with extra factor sqrt(log(1/delta)/log(k)) are both tight up to constants.
results.setup: Exp3-IX from Chapter 12, adversarial bandits x in [0,1]^{n x k}.

results.claim: A bound that holds only for one fixed delta cannot be integrated to an expectation bound better than about n*delta + O(sqrt(kn log(k/delta))), giving O(sqrt(kn log n)) at best, whereas the anytime bound integrates to O(sqrt(kn log k)).
Conjecture (not proved): a policy exists with P(pseudo-regret >= B sqrt(kn) log(1/delta)) <= delta for all nu in E_k.

If an algorithm has expected regret R_n<=B sqrt(kn), then for sufficiently small delta some adversarial bandit gives regret >= c/B sqrt(kn) log(1/(2delta)) with probability at least delta, so Exp3-IX high-probability bounds are nearly tight.

limits: Theorem 17.4 proof is only sketched; details are left to Gerchinovitz and Lattimore 2016 and to Exercise 17.1.

Stochastic bounds are for Gaussian bandits with gaps bounded by one and need the worst-case expected-regret assumption B sqrt((k-1)n); a matching upper bound sqrt(kn) log(1/delta) is only conjectured.
The chapter says nothing about instance-dependent (log n / Delta, UCB-style) bounds; it concerns worst-case sqrt(n) regret. Constants in Theorem 17.4 are unspecified.

practices: When high-probability guarantees are needed at any confidence level, use an anytime algorithm (Exp3-IX bound 17.1), accepting the extra sqrt(log(1/delta)/log k) factor (p.215).

If delta is known in advance, a delta-dependent algorithm gets O(sqrt(kn log(k/delta))), which is tighter, but it cannot be integrated into an expectation bound better than O(sqrt(kn log n)) (p.215-216).
